messages.content: Write a post about starting a mentorship program on an engineering team. Around 250 words.

output:
Clean pass on the slopwatch gate, 266 words.

# Starting a mentorship program on an engineering team

We started ours because two people quit in the same quarter and both exit notes said the same thing: nobody had time for them.

The first version was small on purpose. Six pairs, one hour every two weeks, and a single rule that the mentee owns the agenda. If the mentee shows up with nothing, the meeting ends in ten minutes and that is fine. We wrote no curriculum. Curriculums are where these programs go to die, because someone has to maintain them and nobody wants to.

Matching turned out to be the hard part. Skill overlap is the obvious signal and it is mostly wrong. Our best pair was a backend engineer of four years and a staff engineer who had never touched the service in question. The staff engineer was useful because they had already survived the thing the mentee was in the middle of, which was a reorg, not a codebase.

Two things I would do differently. Ask managers to stay out of it. The first round routed through managers and half the mentees treated the sessions as a performance review with extra steps. And set an end date. Ours ran open-ended, pairs drifted, and people felt guilty about drifting instead of just finishing. Six months with an explicit exit works better than forever with an implied one.

After a year, four of the six original mentees have moved a level. That is not proof of anything. But nobody has written an exit note about time since, and the program costs us three hours a month.
